passages.title: The Voyager Probes
passages.text: Launched in 1977, the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes were originally designed for a five-year mission to study Jupiter and Saturn. Both spacecraft performed so well that NASA extended their missions repeatedly. Voyager 1 is now the most distant human-made object from Earth, having entered interstellar space in 2012. Each probe carries a Golden Record, a phonograph disc containing sounds and images meant to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth, in case either craft is ever found by another civilization.

passages.title: The Library of Alexandria
passages.text: The Library of Alexandria, founded in Egypt in the third century BCE, was one of the largest and most significant libraries of the ancient world. It aimed to collect all the world's knowledge, and scholars there made major advances in mathematics, astronomy, and medicine. The library's exact fate is debated by historians, with damage attributed to several events over centuries rather than a single dramatic fire, as popular legend often suggests.

passages.title: How Octopuses Change Color
passages.text: Octopuses can change the color and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second, using specialized cells called chromatophores. Each chromatophore contains a sac of pigment surrounded by tiny muscles; when the muscles contract, the sac expands and the color becomes more visible. Beneath the chromatophores, other cells called iridophores reflect light to create iridescent blues and greens. Octopuses use this ability both to camouflage against predators and to communicate with other octopuses.

passages.title: Why Ice Floats
passages.text: Most substances are denser as solids than as liquids, but water is an exception. When water freezes, its molecules form a hexagonal crystal lattice that holds them farther apart than in liquid water. This makes ice about nine percent less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats. This property is important for aquatic life: because ice floats and forms an insulating layer on top of lakes and rivers, water below can remain liquid even in freezing temperatures, allowing fish and other organisms to survive winter.

passages.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
passages.text: Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press using movable metal type in the city of Mainz, Germany. Before this, books were copied by hand or printed from carved wooden blocks, making them slow and expensive to produce. Gutenberg's press could produce many identical copies of a text far more quickly, which dramatically lowered the cost of books and helped spread literacy across Europe. His most famous work, the Gutenberg Bible, is considered one of the most important books in history.

passages.title: What Is a Black Hole?
passages.text: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it crosses a boundary called the event horizon. Black holes form when massive stars collapse at the end of their lives. Despite the name, a black hole is not empty; it packs a large amount of mass into a very small space. Scientists cannot observe black holes directly, but they can detect them by observing their effects on nearby stars and gas, or by capturing images of the glowing material that swirls around them.

passages.title: The Discovery of Exoplanets
passages.text: An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun. For centuries, astronomers suspected other stars might have planets, but the first confirmed exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, was not detected until 1995. Many exoplanets are found using the transit method, which measures the tiny dip in a star's brightness as a planet passes in front of it. Thousands of exoplanets have since been confirmed, including some located in the 'habitable zone,' the range of distances from a star where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist.

passages.title: The Rosetta Stone
passages.text: The Rosetta Stone is a granodiorite slab inscribed with the same decree in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Egyptian Demotic script, and Ancient Greek. It was carved in 196 BCE and rediscovered by French soldiers in 1799 near the town of Rosetta in Egypt. Because scholars could already read Ancient Greek, the stone provided the key to finally deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs, a writing system that had been unreadable for centuries. The French scholar Jean-François Champollion completed the decipherment in the 1820s, opening the door to modern Egyptology.

passages.title: Why Leaves Change Color in Autumn
passages.text: Leaves appear green during spring and summer because they are full of chlorophyll, the pigment plants use to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. As days shorten in autumn, trees produce less chlorophyll, and the green color fades. This reveals other pigments that were present in the leaf all along, such as yellow and orange carotenoids. Some trees also produce new red and purple pigments called anthocyanins in autumn, often triggered by bright sunny days combined with cool nights. Eventually, a layer of cells seals off each leaf's stem, and the leaf falls.

passages.title: The Migration of Monarch Butterflies
passages.text: Each autumn, monarch butterflies in eastern North America fly up to 3,000 miles to reach overwintering forests in central Mexico, a journey no single butterfly completes twice. The monarchs that migrate are several generations removed from the ones that made the trip the previous year, yet they return to the same forests their ancestors used, guided by an internal sense of direction linked to the sun's position and Earth's magnetic field. In spring, the surviving butterflies begin the journey north, laying eggs on milkweed plants along the way before a new generation continues onward.

passages.title: How Vaccines Train the Immune System
passages.text: Vaccines work by exposing the immune system to a harmless version or piece of a pathogen, such as a weakened virus or a fragment of its protein coat, without causing the disease itself. In response, the immune system produces antibodies and creates memory cells that 'remember' the pathogen. If the real pathogen is encountered later, these memory cells allow the immune system to respond much faster and more effectively than it would on a first exposure, often preventing illness entirely or making it far milder. Some vaccines require multiple doses because booster shots strengthen and prolong this memory response.

passages.title: The Discovery of Penicillin
passages.text: In 1928, Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from vacation to find that a mold called Penicillium had contaminated one of his bacterial cultures and killed the bacteria around it. Fleming identified the mold's active substance as penicillin, but it took over a decade, and the work of scientists Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, to purify it and produce enough for medical use. Penicillin became the first widely used antibiotic, dramatically reducing deaths from bacterial infections during World War II and afterward. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.
